questions.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 2x2 Symmetric Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-7$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-7.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-7.$ Computing $A-(-7)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+7I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}]+7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $-4{x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -4{x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{17}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{17}}{17} \\ -\frac{4\sqrt{17}}{17}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-1I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{T}\,AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A:$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 4 \\ 4 & -9\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-10.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{T}\,AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A:$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=7\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-10$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 4 \\ 4 & -9\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-10)I & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 4 \\ 4 & -9\end{aligned}]+10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-10)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & -10\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{T}\,AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A:$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=7\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$
